sources.title: David Tong, Electromagnetism, University of Cambridge Part II Mathematical Tripos lecture notes (2026 printing, 236 pp.)
sources.locator: §7 'Matter', printed pp. 172-228 (PDF pp. 180-236): §§7.1-7.6 read in full (polarisation and D pp. 172-178; magnetisation and H pp. 178-183; macroscopic Maxwell equations pp. 183-186; reflection and refraction pp. 186-193; dispersion and Kramers-Kronig pp. 193-205; conductors pp. 205-212) and §7.7 (charge screening pp. 212-228) inspected at heading level, in the retained complete extracted text of the 236-page printing.

contents.name: §7.1 'Electric Fields in Matter': the electrostatic polarisation model, the induced dipole p=αE (7.1) and P=np (7.3)
contents.support: The macroscopic polarisation P as electric dipole moment per unit volume; the scaffolded definition keeps the type, domain, regularity and unit content and drops the microscopic spring model, which is not asserted.

contents.name: §7.1.1 'Polarisation': the bound charge density ρbound=−∇·P (7.5) and the linear response P=ε0χeE (7.4)
contents.support: The bound-charge construction ρb=−divP is part of the definition; the linear susceptibility is not: it is a constitutive branch of the separate closure postulate.

contents.name: §7.1.2 'Electric Displacement': D=ε0E+P (7.6), ∇·D=ρfree (7.7) and the linear-dielectric form D=εE
contents.support: D=ε0E+P is defined on the page; the free-source equation is the separate macroscopic theorem, and the linear form is the closure branch.

contents.name: §7.1.2 'An Example: A Dielectric Sphere': a point charge Q at the centre of a dielectric sphere, screening, E=Q/(4πεr²) (7.8), the induced bound charge and surface-charge discontinuity
contents.reason: This is a central-charge screening configuration, not the uniform applied-field dielectric sphere of this pair; the induced-charge screening argument belongs to electrostatic boundary-value material and was not promised as a pair item, while the pair's sphere example uses the uniform applied field of Fitzpatrick node 71 and Griffiths Example 4.7.

contents.name: §7.2 'Magnetic Fields in Matter': M, the relation B=μ0(H+M) (7.9) and the promise that magnetisation may be treated linearly or may be ferromagnetic
contents.support: M as magnetic dipole moment per unit volume is defined on the page; the linear or ferromagnetic alternatives are model branches and only the constant linear one is adopted by the closure postulate.

contents.name: §7.2.1 'Bound Currents': the bound current Jbound=∇×M (7.10)
contents.support: The bound current density Jb=∂tP+curlM of the definition contains this term; the magnetisation contribution is taken verbatim, with the polarisation-current completion supplied by §7.3.

contents.name: §7.2.2 'Ampère's Law Revisited': H=B/μ0−M (7.11) and ∇×H=Jfree (7.12)
contents.support: H=B/μ0−M is defined on the page; the static Ampere equation becomes the dynamic curl-H macroscopic equation of the separate theorem.

contents.name: §7.3 'Macroscopic Maxwell Equations': the completion of the bound current by ∂P/∂t from bound-charge continuity, ∇×H−∂D/∂t=Jfree and the four equations (7.13)
contents.support: The substitution route and the resulting four equations are exactly the proof route and conclusion of the scaffolded macroscopic theorem, including the bound-source continuity step.

contents.name: §7.3: the linear-material closure D=εE and B=μH as 'the simplest, linear materials', with the warning that ε is not as constant as it is pretended
contents.support: The constant symmetric linear branch of the closure branch is this model choice; the warning motivates the separate memory branch and the explicit restriction to a declared regime.

contents.name: §7.3.1 'A First Look at Waves in Matter': the medium wave equation, v²=1/(εμ) (7.15), the index n=c/v≥1 and B0=k̂×E0/v (7.16)
contents.reason: The medium wave parameters and the plane-wave amplitudes in matter are the declared subject of the wave-interfaces pair (def-em-medium-wave-parameters); this pair does not build wave propagation in media and keeps only the constant-coefficient closure and the isotropic broadband condition εμ≥c⁻².

contents.name: §7.3 'Boundary Conditions': n̂·(D2−D1)=σ (7.17), n̂·(B2−B1)=0 (7.18), n̂×(E2−E1)=0 (7.19) and n̂×(H2−H1)=K (7.20)
contents.support: The four jump identities are the conclusion of the scaffolded theorem, derived there from the distributional macroscopic equations with the explicit one-sided regularity rather than from a limit of smooth solutions.

contents.name: §7.4 'Reflection and Refraction', §7.4.1 'Fresnel Equations' (7.26)-(7.27) and §7.4.2 'Total Internal Reflection'
contents.reason: Reflection and refraction at a dielectric interface are the declared content of the wave-interfaces pair (pthm-em-normal-fresnel, pthm-em-oblique-fresnel); this pair supplies only the interface jumps and the material closure they rest on.

contents.name: §7.5.1-7.5.3 'Dispersion': the oscillator polarisability α(ω) (7.30), the complex wavenumber (7.33)-(7.37), resonant absorption and total reflection
contents.reason: The approved material branch uses an explicitly adopted general causal response kernel and proved dispersion under its stated analytic/subtraction hypotheses; the approved conductor branch has constant scalar Ohmic conductivity. Microscopic oscillator/Drude/plasma-frequency specializations in this source row are not promised by either branch and have no supplied destination. Both general dispersion and constant-Ohmic claims remain intact.

contents.name: §7.5.4 'Causality and the Kramers-Kronig Relation': the causal convolution (7.39)-(7.40), α̃(t)=0 for t<0, analyticity of α(ω) in Imω>0 and the relations (7.45) under the explicit 1/|ω| decay caveat
contents.support: The physics narrative of causality, upper-half-plane analyticity, dispersion relations and the growth caveat is the content of the scaffolded theorem, whose proof is the exact mathematical supplier; the caveat is retained as the stated kernel/growth hypotheses.

contents.name: §7.6.1 'The Drude Model': the DC limit of J(ω)=σ(ω)E(ω) (7.47), i.e. J=σE with real σ
contents.support: The constant-Ohmic conduction branch Jc=σE of the closure postulate absorbs this DC relation; no Drude microscopic derivation, scattering time or frequency-dependent conductivity is taken up on this page.

contents.name: §7.6.1 'The Drude Model': the optical conductivity σ(ω)=σDC/(1−iωτ) (7.48) and its real/imaginary parts
contents.reason: The approved material branch uses an explicitly adopted general causal response kernel and proved dispersion under its stated analytic/subtraction hypotheses; the approved conductor branch has constant scalar Ohmic conductivity. Microscopic oscillator/Drude/plasma-frequency specializations in this source row are not promised by either branch and have no supplied destination. Both general dispersion and constant-Ohmic claims remain intact.

contents.name: §7.6.2-7.6.3 'Electromagnetic Waves in Conductors' and 'Plasma Oscillations': the macroscopic system with free charge and current (7.49)-(7.51), εeff (7.55) and εeff=0 at ωp (7.56)
contents.reason: The approved material branch uses an explicitly adopted general causal response kernel and proved dispersion under its stated analytic/subtraction hypotheses; the approved conductor branch has constant scalar Ohmic conductivity. Microscopic oscillator/Drude/plasma-frequency specializations in this source row are not promised by either branch and have no supplied destination. Both general dispersion and constant-Ohmic claims remain intact.

contents.name: §7.6.4 'Dispersion Relations in Quantum Mechanics': E=ℏω and p=ℏk
contents.reason: Quantum dispersion relations import quantum mechanics into a classical electromagnetic framework and are outside the classical-electromagnetism scope; the classical dispersion relations of this pair are the Kramers-Kronig statements, which make no quantum claim.

contents.name: §7.7 'Charge Screening': Debye-Hückel screening (7.58)-(7.61), the dielectric function (7.62)-(7.66), Thomas-Fermi (7.67)-(7.71), Lindhard (7.72)-(7.73) and Friedel oscillations (7.74)
contents.reason: The screening section requires statistical mechanics (Boltzmann and Fermi-Dirac distributions, chemical potential) and later quantum theory, which the classical-electromagnetism framework does not supply; only the headings were inspected and no screening claim is built.

contents.name: §4.3.3 'Boundary Conditions' (printed p. 178): the normal-D and tangential-E boundary conditions in terms of D and E
contents.support: The normal-D and tangential-E jump conditions are two of the four conclusions of the scaffolded theorem, proved there from the distributional identities rather than by a limiting pillbox.

contents.name: §4.4.1 'Susceptibility, Permittivity, Dielectric Constant' (printed pp. 179-181), equations (4.30)-(4.34): P=ε0χeE, D=εE, εr=1+χe and the statement that this is a model of many but not all substances
contents.support: The constant linear branch of the closure postulate is this model choice; the text's warning that it is not universal supports the explicit restriction and the exclusion of ferroelectric and nonlinear response.

contents.name: §4.4.2 'Boundary Value Problems with Linear Dielectrics' (printed pp. 186-188), Example 4.7: the dielectric sphere in a uniform field, the two boundary conditions and the interior field
contents.support: The example's potentials, matching conditions and uniform interior field are exactly the sphere content; the scaffolded example uses absolute permittivities, verifies the jump conditions and adds the uniqueness certification in a declared decay class.

contents.name: §4.4.3 'Energy in Dielectric Systems' (printed pp. 191-193), equations (4.55)-(4.58): ΔW=∫(ΔD)·E valid for any material and W=½∫D·E for linear dielectrics, with the two interpretations of assembly work
contents.support: The stored-energy density and the restriction to linear response are the content of the scaffolded item; its scope clause keeps the same linearity restriction and excludes dispersive and hysteretic storage.

contents.name: §4.4.4 'Forces on Dielectrics' (printed pp. 193-196): mechanical force computations on dielectric bodies
contents.reason: Mechanical forces on dielectrics require a material mechanical model and are not part of the response-and-interface scope of this pair; no force, stress or electromechanical claim is built here.

contents.name: §6.2 'The Field of a Magnetized Object', §6.2.1 'Bound Currents', §6.2.2 'Physical Interpretation of Bound Currents' and §6.2.3 'The Magnetic Field Inside Matter' (printed pp. 263-269): M, Jb=∇×M and the bound-current interpretation
contents.support: The magnetisation and bound-current definitions are those of the scaffolded definition item; the physical interpretation is motivation and the actual microscopic mechanism is not asserted.

contents.name: §6.3 'The Auxiliary Field H', §6.3.1 'Ampere's Law in Magnetized Materials' and §6.3.2 'A Deceptive Parallel' (printed pp. 269-273): ∇×H=Jf and the warning that ∇·H is not itself a free-source equation
contents.support: The curl-H macroscopic equation and the scope warning are the content absorbed by the scaffolded theorem's clause (b) and its scope clause (c).

contents.name: §6.3.3 'Boundary Conditions' (printed p. 273): the normal-B and tangential-H boundary conditions
contents.support: The normal-B and tangential-H jump conditions are the remaining two conclusions of the scaffolded theorem, with the free sheet current Kf appearing in n×[H].

contents.name: §6.4 'Linear and Nonlinear Media', §6.4.1 'Magnetic Susceptibility and Permeability' (printed pp. 274-278): M=χmH, B=μH for linear media
contents.support: The constant linear magnetic branch B=μH of the closure postulate is this content; the anisotropy and nonlinearity warnings are handled by the explicit matrix branch and the stated exclusions.

contents.name: §6.4.2 'Ferromagnetism' (printed pp. 278-284): hysteresis, saturation and the absence of a single-valued B-H relation
contents.reason: Ferromagnetic hysteresis and saturation are outside the declared constant linear and memory branches of this pair; the scope clauses of the closure and energy items record that no instantaneous or single-valued response is claimed for them.

contents.name: §7.1.1 'Ohm's Law' (printed pp. 285-292): J=σf with the resistivity and the ohmic heating rate
contents.support: The constant-Ohmic conduction branch Jc=σE of the closure postulate absorbs this phenomenological law; no microscopic conductivity model and no temperature dependence is taken up.

contents.name: §7.3.5 'Maxwell's Equations in Matter' (printed pp. 328-331), equations (7.49)-(7.55): the free/bound/polarisation-current separation and the Maxwell system in matter
contents.support: The substitution route and the resulting four equations are exactly the scaffolded theorem's content and proof route.

contents.name: §7.3.6 'Boundary Conditions' (printed pp. 331-333), equations (7.59)-(7.64): the four general boundary conditions and their linear-medium and source-free specialisations
contents.support: The four jump conditions in the general source-carrying form are the conclusion of the scaffolded theorem; the linear-medium elimination there is the interface example's content.
